Bomb blasts and terrorist activities in the country 
 *122. SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR: 
  SHRI NAND KISHORE YADAV: †† 
 Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) the number and details of bomb blas ts and terrorist activities that took  
place in the country between 1st January, 2008 to  31st January, 2009, State-wise and incident-
wise separately; 
 (b) the details of the persons killed and injured, State-wise; 
 (c) the ex-gratia payment made to them, State and incident-wise; and 
 (d) the action taken during the said peri od to strengthen the security of the  
nation? 
 THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
 (a) and (b) Apart from violence in the areas affected by militancy, insurgency and extremist 
activities, viz., Jammu and Kashmir, some of the No rth-Eastern States and some States 
affected by naxalite activities, terrorist attacks an d incidents have also occurred in various parts 
of the country between 1st January, 2008 and 31st January, 2009. Based on available 
information, a statement showing major incidents of  terrorist attacks including bomb blasts that 
have occurred in the above period in some pa rts of the hinterland in the country, alongwith 
number of persons including secu rity personnel killed and number of persons injured is given 
below:—

 As per available information, in the attack  on CRPF Group Centre, Rampur, 7 security 
personnel were killed out of the 8 persons killed;  in the bomb blasts in Jaipur, 3 security 
personnel were killed out of the 69 persons killed and in the terrorist attacks in Mumbai, 18 
security personnel were killed out of the 164 persons killed. 
 (c) Ex-gratia relief and assistance is generally announced by the State Governments to 
victims of terrorist violence. The details of such ex-gratia paid in all cases of terrorist/extremist/ 
naxal violence are not centrally compiled and maintained. 
 The Central Government, however, reimburses to the State of Jammu  and  Kashmir, North 
Eastern States and naxal affected States toward s expenditure incurred by them for this purpose 
as per the extant policy of the Government. The Central Government has also launched a 
scheme in 2008 towards this end. The broad aim of the scheme is to assist victims of terrorist 
and communal violence. Under the scheme, financial assistance of Rs. 3 lac is admissible to the 
family member (s) in the event of death or permanent incapacitation of the breadwinner/ 
householder of the family. The  scheme  also provides for a health card to be given by the District 

 3
Health Society, functioning under the National  Rural Health Mission to those permanently 
incapacitated, to entitle them to free medical treatment in respect to injuries due to violence. 
 (d) The Government has been pursuing a mult i-pronged strategy to deal with terrorism, 
and a variety of measures have been taken to strengthen the security arrangements in this 
context. These, inter-alia, include assistance to the State Governments under the Scheme for 
Modernisation of State Police Forces (MPF) fo r strengthening police related infrastructure, 
equipments, weaponry, mobility, training and stre ngthening of the State Intelligence machinery; 
assistance for raising India Reserve Battalions (w ith provision for raising 2 Coys as Commando 
Units); reimbursement of various types of security expenditure incurred by the State 
Governments under the Security Related Expenditure (SRE) Scheme; deployment of Central 
Para-Military Forces to aid and assist the State Police to deal with specific situations; sharing of 
intelligence and operational coordination with the State Governments in this regard, etc. In 
addition, several measures have been taken at the Central level for strengthening the internal 
security apparatus. These, inter-alia, include; substantial expansion of the Central  
Para-Military Forces (CPMFs) in the recent years,  including a decision to raise 10 Specialised 
Command Battalions in the CRPF, along with action for modernization of the CPMFs; substantial 
augmentation and strengthening of the intelligen ce machinery by sanction of additional posts 
and strengthening of institutional mechanisms  for sharing of intelligence and operational 
coordination with the States; construction of roads and fencing, with flood lighting, on the Indo-
Pakistan and Indo-Bangladesh borders, togeth er with provision of modern surveillance 
equipment; with a view to checking infiltration smuggling and other illegal cross border activities; 
launching of scheme for coastal security under wh ich assistance is being provided to the States 
for setting up Police Stations and boats, jeeps and motorcycles for sea and land patrolling; and, 
steps for expanding the infrastructure for genera l and specialized training for the State police 
personnel, including action for setting up 20 Counter-Insurgency and Anti-Terrorism Schools. A 
decision has also been taken to establish 4 NSG Hubs in Chennai, Hyderabad, Kolkata and 
Mumbai with a view to enabli ng speedy movement to the affected area in the event of 
emergency. Towards the end the Government/NSG have also been given powers to requisition 
Civil aircraft in case of need. 
 Apart from the above, the Unlawful Activiti es Prevention (Amendment) Act, 2008 has been 
enacted with a view to strengthening the legal fr amework for dealing with terrorist activities. The 
National Investigation Agency Act, 2008 has also  been passed and the National Investigation 
Agency has been constituted to investigate and pr osecute certain types of offences relating to 
legislations included in the Schedule to the Act. An Ordinance has also been issued enabling the 
deployment of CISF in Joint sector/Private sector units keeping in view of their criticality from the 
security angle. 
 The security arrangements to deal with va rious internal security challenges, including 
terrorism, are being continuously reviewed with a view to taking action for further strengthening 
and streamlining, etc., as found necessary, from time to time.

 SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM:  Sir, I think, we should make a distinction between terrorist 
threats, infiltration by terrorists and other illega l activities like smuggling currency, etc. This 
question concerns terrorist threats. I have said repeatedly that India faces terrorist threats. Given

 SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, I have gone through the reply given by the hon. Minister 
stating therein what measures the Government ha s taken to contain terrorism. I have only one 
question to put to the hon. Minister. I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether the 
Government has studied the reasons for no further attacks on the United States of America after 
the attack on the Twin Towers. In the case of  Israel, they have also taken such measures 
whereby further attacks have been avoided. Has the Government gone into these issues? I 
would also like to know whether the measures wh ich were taken in the USA and Israel are being 
taken in our country. 
 SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM:  Sir, I am grateful to the hon. Member for putting this question. 
Yes, we have studied the measures taken by the United States after the September 11 attack. Of 
course, the United States being a wealthier and richer country, has spent billions of dollars for 
putting together a very effective counter-intelligence and counter-terrorist apparatus and 
brought it under the Department of Homeland Secu rity. A team from India was invited to visit 
there. A team did visit the United States and studied their National Centre for Counter Terrorism. 
The team has come back. We have taken whatev er elements are relevant and germane to the 
Indian situation. Notwithstanding some financial constraints, we have tried to replicate the NCCT 
through our MAC which is now the nodal centre for counter terrorism. We should spend some 
more money. But more money has been made available in 2009-10. We are also working with 
some other security agencies of other countries an d Israel is one of them. But Israel is not the 
only one, there are other countries which have o ffered to work with us and we are working with 
them. In this context, I would like to mentio n the United Kingdom and Germany also. We are 
learning every day. I can say with some humility that we are improving every day. But there is still 
some distance to go. I think by the 31st of Marc h, connectivity between MAC, the subsidiary-
MAC and the Special Branch of the Police will be established. Data Centres will be established 
by May, 2009. If everyone cooperates and supports the Government, as I am getting it today 
from the State Governments, we will be better pl aced, say by March than we are today; we will 
be better placed in May than we will be in Marc h. These are steps which have to be taken every 
month, every week. I am confident that our leve l of preparedness will improve as every week 
passes by.

Protection of jobs of displaced persons due to global economic melt down 
 *128. SHRI RUDRA NARAYAN PANY: 
  SHRI M. RAMA JOIS: 
 Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
 (a) how many workers in the country have lost their jobs due to the recent global 
economic melt down; 
 (b) the Ministry’s estimation about the job loss es in the country in the current year because 
of this; and 
 (c) the steps contemplated to protect jobs and help the displaced workers? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINIST RY OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI 
OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) and (b) The estimates of employment and unemployment are 
obtained through quinquennial labour force surveys conducted by National Sample Survey 
Organisation. Last such survey was conducted during 2004-05. However, with a view to assess 
impact of economic slowdown on employment in the industries/sectors presumed to be 
adversely affected by the slowdown during the period October, 2008 — January, 2009, Ministry 
of Labour and  Employment carried out a survey in important sectors, viz. Mining, Textiles, 
Metals, Gems and  Jewellery, Automobile, Tran sport and IT/BPO. These sectors contributed 
more than 60% to GDP in the year 2007-08. It has been revealed that about 5.89 lakh workers 
have lost their jobs during October, 2008 — January, 2009. The major impact of the slowdown is 
noticed in the export oriented units. 
 (c) Government is concerned about the impact  of global financial crises on the Indian 
economy and several measures — financial and fisc al — have been initiated to instill confidence 
in the economy, spur growth and overcome crisis. Some of the important steps relate to RBI 
measures to enhance liquidity in the market an d two economic packages by the Government of 
India, mainly comprising additional spending, in terest subvention and excise duty cuts. These 
measures will  prevent large scale Job losses. In order to  provide a  social safety net,  with effect

 34
from 01-04-2005, the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation has introduced “Rajiv Gandhi 
Shramik Kalyan Yojana ”. Under the scheme, employees who lose their employment due to 
retrenchment, closure of factories/establis hments or permanent invalidity due to non-
employment injury, after being insured for five or more years, are entitled to unemployment 
allowance in cash equal to 50% of their wage for six months during his/her entire service. This 
entitlement has recently been increased to one ye ar. In addition, he and his family members are 
also entitled to medical care. 
 A new scheme called ‘Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP)’ 
announced in August, 2008 for implementation  from 2008-09 to 2012-13 is being implemented 
with an estimated expenditure of Rs. 4735 crore towards margin money and Rs. 250 crore 
towards backward forward linkage s with the target for generati on of 37.37 lakh additional 
employment opportunities.

 *129. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to

 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V. RADHIKA 
SELVI): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. A comprehensiv e Coastal Security Scheme was approved in 
January, 2005 for implementation over a five year period commencing 2005-06. The scheme was 
formulated on the basis of the recommendations of the Group of Minister on ‘Reforming the 
National Security System’, an d in consultation with all agencies concerned and State 
Governments, including Tamil Nadu. 
 The Coastal Security Scheme, which is supplem ental in nature, aims at enhancing coastal 
security by strengthening infrastructure for patr olling and surveillance of the coastal areas. It is 
being implemented in nine coastal States, viz. Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, 
Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa and West Bengal, and four coastal Union Territories, viz. 
Daman and Diu, Lakshadweep, Pondicherry an d Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Under the

have been approved. The Police Stations will be provided with 204 patrol boats fitted with

312 motorcycles for patrolling along the coast. A lu mp sum assistance of Rs. 10 lakhs per police 
station is also provided for computers and equipments, etc.

expenditure and Rs. 151 crores for recurring expe nditure on fuel, maintenance and repairs of

BPL persons in the country 
 *135. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Mi nister of RURAL DEVEL OPMENT be pleased 
to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that out of 30 cr ore persons Below Poverty Line (BPL) in the 
country, about 22 crore, i.e. 73 per cent live in rural areas; 
 (b) whether Government has so far examined reasons for rural poverty; 
 (c) whether Government has set up any mechanism to verify the actual BPL list (State-
wise); and 
 (d) the steps Government has taken so far to achieve “Millennium Development Goal of 
eardicating extreme hunger and poverty ” under its various schemes like NREGA, IGNOAPS, 
SGSY etc. by 2015? 
 THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI R. RAGHUVANSH PRASAD SINGH): 
(a) Yes Sir. According to poverty estimates of Planning Commission released for the year 2004-
05 based on the Sample Survey Data on Hous ehold Consumer Expenditure (NSS 61st Round), 
30.17 crore people were living below the poverty line out of which 22.09 crore (73.22%) were in 
rural areas. 
 (b) and (c) The Eleventh Five Year Plan Do cument analyses the reasons for rural poverty 
which includes unemployment and under-employment, lack of access to natural resources, over 
dependence on agriculture, besides chronic social factors. While the estimation of poverty in the 
Country is done by the Planning Commission, the Ministry of Rural Development provides 
financial and technical assistan ce to the States/UTs to conduct the Below Poverty Line (BPL) 
Census generally in the beginning of  a  Five  Year  Plan  with  the  objective  to  identify  the  BPL

 40
families living the rural areas who could be targ eted under its programmes. Last BPL Census 
2002 was conducted for the Tenth Five Year Plan which was based on the methodology of Score 
Based Ranking of the Rural Households for wh ich 13 Socio Economic Parameters were used. 
The BPL list so prepared by the States is to be approved by the Gram Sabha in its open 
meeting. For redressing the public grievanc es, a two-stage appeal mechanism was also 
provided. In order to ensure transparency, the States have been requested to keep the printed 
copies of the BPL list at the Village Panchayat level and also to post it on the public domain 
besides painting of IAY Permanent Waitlist on the wall of the common building. About 16 States 
have already posted the BPL data either on the State website or on the website of the Ministry of 
Rural Development. 
 (d) The first Millennium Development Goal (MDG) envisages eradication of extreme 
poverty and hunger with the target to halve the proportion of people whose income is less than 
one dollar a day between 1990 and 2015. Keeping in view a large number of people living below 
the poverty line in the Country and the MDGs, Government has resorted to direct intervention for 
poverty reduction through various programmes spec ially focusing on generation of employment, 
development of rural infrastructure, strength ening of rural livelihood and providing basic 
amenities to the rural people. The present progr ammes of the Ministry of Rural Development 
such as, National Rural Employment Guarante e Act (NREGA), Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar 
Yojana (SGSY), Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS) and Indira Awaas 
Yojana (IAY) are the steps towards eradicat ion of rural poverty and to achieve the  
MDGs of eradication of extreme poverty and hunger as well. The NREGA guarantees 100 days of 
wage employment to all the rura l households in a financial year  whose adult members volunteer 
to do the manual work. Under this programme , employment of 90.50 crore persondays was 
generated during 2006-07. During 2007-08 and 2008-09 (upto January ’09) employment of 
143.59 crore persondays and 152.12 crore pers ondays was generated,  respectively. Under 
SGSY about 32 lakh Self Help Groups (SHGs) have been formed since 1999 and 115 lakh 
Swarozgaris were provided economic assistance to  set up income generating activities. Under 
Indira Awaas Yojana, more than 63 lakh houses ha ve been constructed for the rural poor during 
the last four years which provides better living environment to them. Under IGNOAPS it is 
anticipated that over 150 lakh beneficiaries will be covered during 2008-09. 
 The Ministry of Rural Development has proposed to restructure the self-employment 
programme of SGSY for its implementation in a mission mode and in a time bound manner with 
placement based skill development as one of majo r components. The objective is to provide 
sustainable employment to the rural poor and to step up the pace of eradication of poverty in the 
country.

to be issued by the State Govern ments during recruitment in Army;

providing domicile certificates for recruitment in Ar my, since it is an issue of national security; 
and

 THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI A.K. ANTONY): (a) to (d) A few instances of 
candidates attempting to get recruited in the Army on the basis of fake domicile certificates have 
been reported. The recruiting officers have been instructed to be vigilant. Stringent verification 
measures are in force to scrutini ze the domicile/nationality, age and education qualification etc. 
of all candidates appearing for recruitment in Defence Forces. The domicile certificates issued by 
civil authorities are checked during various stages  of recruitment and the candidates with fake 
domicile certificates are not permitted to atte nd the recruitment rally. Further, character and 
antecedents of the recruits are verified through the respective police/intelligence authorities. The 
State Governments have been requested to keep a vigil against candidates trying to get through

offices.

However, the inflows in October-December, 2008 have shown a decline. 
 (c) Various studies by international agencies and world wide analysis have assessed that 
the FDI flows to developing economies would generally decline. 
 Under the liberalised economic environment, investment decisions of investors are based 
on macro-economic policy framework, investment  climate in the host country, investment 
policies of the trans-national corporations an d other commercial considerations. Government 
has put in place a liberal and investor-friendly policy on FDI under which FDI up to 100% is

Success of NREGA 
 *138. SHRI RAJNITI PRASAD: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, (NREGA) the 
ambitious scheme of Government to provide income to the rural poor has not been as successful 
as intended; 
 (b) whether it is also a fact that the job card s prepared for the beneficiaries are kept by the 
Gram Pradhans and the money that is meant to be given to them is actually not given; and 
 (c) if so, the steps Government would take  to minimise the leakage in the scheme? 
 THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD SINGH): (a) 
No, Sir. NREGA has been successful in fulfillm ent of its objectives of augmentation of 
employment opportunities and creation of durable assets. So far in the current year, nearly 4 
crore households have got employment under NREGA. Persondays generation under NREGA 
has been almost two times of the persondays  generation in the earlier wage employment 
programmes. A significant share in the employ ment generated belongs to SCs (30%), STs 
(25%) and women (48%). 22 lakh works have been  taken up in the current financial year of 
which 46% relate to water conservation, 18 % to rural connectivity and 15% to land 
development. Individual land owned by 4.36 lakh households belonging to SC/ST, BPL and IAY 
have been benefited from NREGA works such as  irrigation facility, land development and 
plantation. 
 (b) No, Sir. Para 2 of Schedule-II of NREG Act provides that all job cards shall be in the 
custody of the job card holders to whom they be long. Ministry of Rural Development has also 
issued instructions from time to time in this regard. However, seven instances have been 
brought to the notice of the Ministry regarding job cards being kept in the custody of Gram 
Pradhans which have been sent to the State Governments for suitable action. 
 (c) In order to minimise leak ages in the implementation of NREGA, the Ministry has taken 
the following steps:— 
 (I) Generating Awareness  
  It is the constant endeavor of the Gove rnment to generate greater awareness among 
rural households about their legal rights under NREGA through intensive IEC activities. 
The efforts made in this regard involve print as well as electronic media such as 
brochures, people’s primers, hand books,  TV spots, radio jingles, advertisements, 
films etc. Gram Sabhas have been conven ed. Village camps have been organized by 
the District teams and Self Help Groups associated with awareness generation 
campaign. Government  of  India  has  also  introduced awards  known  as  Rozgar 

 43
   Jagrookta Puraskar to recognize the ou tstanding contributions by the Civil Society 
Organizations (CSOs) for promoting effectiv e implementation of NREGA in different 
States of the Country. In the NREGA Samm elan held on 2.2.2009, five such NGOs 
have been awarded Rozgar Jagrookta Purask ar for their outstanding contributions in 
the field of awareness generation. 
 (II) Transparency and strict Vigilance  and  Monitoring 
 (i) Payment of wages to the NREGA worker s has been made statutory through their 
accounts in Banks/post offices. So far 6.15 crore accounts of NREGA workers in 
Banks/Post Offices have been opened. 
 (ii) Mandatory social audit of works has be en provided under the Act. So far, Social 
Audit has been conducted in 2.20 lakh Gram Panchayats. 
 (iii) Ministry has prescribed regular veri fication of the works being executed under 
NREGA. So far 2.99 lakh works have been verified by district level officials and 
17.38 lakh works have been verified by block level officials. 
 (III) MIS  
  A comprehensive web based MIS has been implemented which places all data relating 
to financial and programme performance indicators in public domain. 1.2 crore muster 
rolls and 6.1 crore job cards are available on the website. 
 (IV) Capacity building and Peoples’ participation 
 (i) NREGA has empowered the Panchayati Raj Institutions by way of capacity 
building of the functionaries, providing additional manpower, ICT support and by 
implementation of the programme through PRIs. 1.96 lakh Gram Rozgar Sahayaks 
have been appointed at the Gram Panchaya t level and a pool of technical staff is 
deployed at the Block and district level including 23,501 technical staff; 7070 Data 
Entry Operators; and 5574 Accountants. 
 (ii) For ensuring people participation, Village level Monitoring Committees have  
been set up and about 7.41 lakh memb ers of these Committees have been 
trained. 
 (V) Accountability 
 (i) State Governments are to set up a Hi gh level Coordination Committee under the 
Chief Secretary of the State to ensure inter-departmental coordination in the 
implementation of the Act. The Co mmittee shall regularly review the 
implementation of Schemes and ensure that 2%, 10% and 100% of the 
inspection of the works an d records of the Scheme at the State/District/Block 
respectively is conducted once a quarter and all deficiencies are removed and all 
grievances are redressed. 
 (ii) District Programme Coordinator are to ensure that within 15 days of funds 
received by them, the same is released to eligible Gram Panchayat in the District. 

 44
 (iii) District Collectors have been made re sponsible for the proper organization of the 
Gram Sabha wherever required under the Act. 
 (iv) The Gram Sabha and Ward Sabha are to  identify and select the projects to be 
taken up in the Gram Panchayat. Gram Sabha will be held regularly to ensure 
social audit. All information relating to flow of funds, works, workers, muster rolls, 
measurement books, sancti on orders, cash book and all other records and 
registers shall be placed in the Gram Sa bha. There shall be video documentation 
of the proceedings of all Gram Sabhas.

Genetically modified food products 
 857. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
  SHRI ISHWAR SINGH: 
 Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government is aware that import ed Genetically Modified (GM) food products 
are entering Indian supermarkets and food chains unchecked; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; 
 (c) whether Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) has taken any action to check 
the illegal entry of GM food products; and 
 (d) if so, the details thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DE PARTMENT OF COMMER CE, MINISTRY OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) to (d) As per the Foreign Trade 
Policy, the import of Genetically Modified Organism (GMOs) and Living Modified Organisms 
(LMOs) for the purpose of (i) Research  and  Development (R & D); (ii) Food; (iii) Feed;  
(iv) Processing in Bulk and (v) for Environment release will be governed by the provisions  
of the Environment Protection Act 1986 and Rules 1989. The import of any Food, Feed, raw  or 

 51
processed or any ingredient of food, food addi tives or any food product that contains GM 
material and is being used either for Industri al production, Environmen tal release, or field 
application will be allowed only with the approval of the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee 
(GEAC). Institutes/Companies who wish to import GM material for R and D purposes will 
submit their proposal to the Review Committe e for Genetic Modification (RCGM) under the 
Department of Bio-Technology. In case the Companies/Institutes use these Genetically Modified 
material for commercial purposes, approval of GEAC  is also required. At the time of import, all 
consignments containing products, which have been subjected to Genetic Modification, will 
carry a declaration stating that the product is Ge netically Modified. In case a consignment does 
not carry such a declaration and is later found to  contain GM material, the importer is liable to 
penal action under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act 1992.

Change in WTO proposals 
 865. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Mi nister of COMMERCE  AND INDUSTRY be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that Government had pressed for change in WTO proposals in the 
interest of our farmers and nascent industries during hard negotiation in Geneva in May, 2008; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; and 
 (c) the ultimate outcome of the discussions? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DE PARTMENT OF COMMER CE, MINISTRY OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) Throughout the Doha 
Round negotiations on agriculture and Non-Agri cultural Market Access (NAMA) at the World 
Trade Organisation (WTO), India has been voicing its concerns strongly, wherever it felt that the 
proposals under consideration had fallen short of its expectations and requirements. 
 In the agriculture negotiations, substantial an d effective reductions in domestic support and 
tariffs in agriculture by developed countries, while enabling developing countries to protect and 
promote the interests of their low income and reso urce poor farmers, is a key priority for India. 
India has been working closely with its developing country partners in the G-20 and G-33 
coalitions towards this end. 
 In the negotiations on NAMA, India, alon g with its coalition partners in the  
NAMA 11, has been negotiating for flexibilities that are both adequate and appropriate for 
protecting its sensitive sectors and nascent indust ries from the impact of tariff reductions or 
bindings. 
 (c) The Doha Round of trade negotiations is  still in progress. A mini-Ministerial meeting 
was held at the WTO in July, 2008 with the objective of finalizing agriculture and NAMA 
modalities. The meeting, however, ended without reaching an agreement, because while 
progress was made on some issues, there were many others that could not be discussed at all 
or on which there were persisting differences amongst Members. Based on subsequent 
discussions at the WTO, revised draft proposal s were issued on 6 December, 2008, which will 
be further discussed and negotiated.

(d) Government has issued, on February 13, 2009, Press Note 2 of 2009 on Guidelines for 
calculation of total foreign investment i.e. direct and indirect foreign investment in Indian 
companies and Press Note 3 of 2009 on Guidelines for transfer of ownership or control of Indian 
companies in sectors with caps from resident In dian citizens to non-resident entities. These 
guidelines were considered by a Group of Ministers and approved by the Cabinet Committee on 
Economic Affairs. 
 The salient features of Press Note 2 of 2009 on  Guidelines for calculation of total foreign 
investment i.e. direct and indirect foreign investment in Indian companies are:— 
 (i) All investment directly by a non-resident entity into the Indian company would be 
counted towards foreign investment. 
 (ii) The foreign investment through the investing Indian company would not be considered 
for calculation of the indirect foreign invest ment in case of Indian companies which are 
‘owned and controlled’ by resident Indian citizens and/or Indian Companies which are 
‘owned and controlled’ ultimately by resident Indian citizens. 
 (iii) For cases where this condition is not sati sfied or if the investing company is owned or 
controlled by ‘non resident en tities’, the entire investment by the investing company 
into the subject Indian Company would be considered as indirect foreign investment. 
 (iv) As an exception, the indirect foreign investment in only the 100% owned subsidiaries 
of operating-cum-investing/investing comp anies, will be limited to the foreign 
investment in the operating-cum-investing/investing company. 
 Press Note 3 of 2009, on the guidelines on transfer of ownership or control of Indian 
companies in sectors with caps, from resident In dian citizens to non-re sident entities, would 
ensure that, in sectors with caps, Government ap proval/FIPB approval would be required in all 
cases where an Indian company is being establis hed with foreign investment and is owned or 
controlled by a non-resident entity; or the owners hip or control of an existing Indian company, 
currently owned or controlled by resident Indian citizens and Indian companies, which are owned 
or controlled by resident Indian citizens, will be/is being transferred/passed on to a non-resident 
entity as a consequence of transfer of shares to non-resident entities through amalgamation, 
merger, acquisition etc. 
 The adoption of guidelines contained in Pr ess Note 2 of 2009 will simplify, streamline and 
rationalize the methodology of calculation of indirect foreign investment across sectors leading to 
investor friendly, credible and predictable regulations. This would facilitate greater foreign capital

inflows and send a positive signal in the presen t difficult economic scenario. The adoption of 
guidelines contained in Press Note 3 of 2009 wo uld ensure that approval of Government of 
India/FIPB would be required for establishment/change in ownership or control of an Indian 
company from resident Indian citizens to non-resident entities in sectors with sectoral caps.

Statement 
Findings and Recommendations of ICRIER 
 The real GDP is expected to grow at 8-10 pe r cent per annum in the next five years. As a 
result, the consuming class with annual household incomes above Rs. 90,000 is expected to rise 
from about 370 million in 2006-07 to 620 million in 2011-12. Consequently, the retail business in 
India is estimated to grow at 13 per cent an nually from US$ 322 billion in 2006-07 to US$ 590 
billion in 2011-12. The study shows:— 
 • The unorganized retail sector is expected to grow at about 10 per cent per annum with 
sales rising from US$ 309 billion in 2006-07 to US$ 496 billion in 2011-12. 
 • Given the relatively weak financial Stat e of unorganized retailers, and the physical 
space constraints on their expansion prospects,  this sector alone will not be able to 
meet the growing demand for retail. 
 • Hence, organized retail which now constitutes a small four per cent of total retail sector 
is likely to grow at a much faster pace of  45-50 per cent per annum and quadruple its 
share in total retail trade to 16 per cent by 2011-12. 
 • This represents a positive sum game in which both unorganized and organized retail 
not only coexist but also grow substantially in size. 
 • The majority of unorganized retailers survey ed in this study, indicated their preference 
to continue in the business and compete rather than exit. 
The Empirical Basis 
 The study comprised of survey of all segments of the economy that could be affected by the 
entry of large corporates in the retail business. The findings are based on a survey of 2020 
unorganized small retailers across 10 major cities; 1318 consumers shopping at both organized 
and unorganized retail outlets; 100 intermediaries; and 197 farmers. In addition, a “control 
sample” survey was done of 805 unorganized retailers who are not in the vicinity of organized 
retail outlets in four metro cities. 

 78 
 Detailed interviews were also carried out fo r 12 large manufacturers, 20 small manufacturers 
and six established modern retailers. 
 The study contains an extensive review of in ternational retail experience, particularly from 
the major emerging market economies. 
Main Findings 
 Impact on Unorganized Retailers 
 • Unorganized retailers in the vicinity of or ganized retailers experienced a decline in their 
volume of business and profit in the init ial years after the entry of large organized 
retailers. 
 • The adverse impact on sales and profit weakens over time. 
 • There was no evidence of a decline in over all employment in the unorganized sector as 
a result of the entry of organized retailers. 
 • There is some decline in employment in the North and West regions which, however, 
also weakens over time. 
 • The rate of closure of unorganized retail shops in gross terms is found to be 4.2 per 
cent per annum which is much lower than th e international rate of closure of small 
businesses. 
 • The rate of closure on account of competit ion from organized retail is lower still at  
1.7 per cent per annum. 
 • There is competitive response from trad itional retailers through improved business 
practices and technology upgradation. 
 • A majority of unorganized retailers is keen  to stay in the business and compete, while 
also wanting the next generation to continue likewise. 
 • Small retailers have been extending more  credit to attract and retain customers. 
 • However, only 12 per cent of unorganized re tailers have access to institutional credit 
and 37 per cent felt the need for better access to commercial bank credit. 
 • Most unorganized retailers are committed to remaining independent and barely 10 per 
cent preferred to become franchisees of organized retailers. 
 Impact on Consumers  
 • Consumers have definitely gained from organized retail on multiple counts. 
 • Overall consumer spending has increased  with the entry of the organized retail. 

 79 
 • While all income groups saved through organized retail purchases, the survey revealed 
that lower income consumers saved more. Thus, organized retail is relatively more 
beneficial to the less well-off consumers. 
 • Proximity is a major comparative advantage of unorganized outlets. 
 • Unorganized retailers have significant co mpetitive strengths that include consumer 
goodwill, credit sales, amenability to bargaini ng, ability to sell loose items, convenient 
timings, and home delivery. 
 Impact on Intermediaries  
 • The study did not find any evidence so fa r of adverse impact of organized retail on 
intermediaries. 
 • There is, however, some adverse impact on turnover and profit  of intermediaries 
dealing in products such as, fruit, vegetables, and apparel. 
 • Over two-thirds of the intermediaries plan  to expand their businesses in response to 
increased business opportunities opened by the expansion of retail. 
 • Only 22 per cent do not want the next generation to enter the same business. 
 Impact on Farmers 
 • Farmers benefit significantly from the opti on of direct sales to organized retailers. 
 • Average price realization for cauliflower fa rmers selling directly to organized retail is 
about 25 per cent higher than their procee ds from sale to regulated Government 
mandi. 
 • Profit realization for farmers selling direct ly to organized retailers is about 60 per cent 
higher than that received from selling in the mandi. 
 • The difference is even larger when th e amount charged by the commission agent 
(usually 10 per cent of sale price) in the mandi is taken into account. 
 Impact on Manufacturers  
 • Large manufacturers have started feeling the competitive impact of organized retail 
through price and payment pressures. 
 • Manufacturers have responded through building and reinforcing their brand strength, 
increasing their own retail presence, ‘adopting’ small retailers, and setting up 
dedicated teams to deal with modern retailers. 
 • Entry of organized retail is transforming the logistics industry. This will create significant 
positive externalities across the economy. 
 • Small manufacturers did not report any significant impact of organized retail. 

 80 
Policy Recommendations 
 On the basis of the results of the surveys an d the review of international retail experience, 
the study makes the following major recommendations:— 
 1. Modernization of wetmarkets through public-private partnerships. 
 2. Facilitate cash-and-carry outlets, like Metro, for sale to unorganized retail and 
procurement from farmers, as in China. 
 3. Encourage co-operatives and associatio ns of unorganized retailers for direct 
procurement from suppliers and farmers. 
 4. Ensure better credit availability to unorganized retailers from banks and  
micro-credit institutions through innovative banking solutions. 
 5. Facilitate the formation of farmers’ co-ope ratives to directly sell to organized retailers. 
 6. Encourage formulation of “private codes of conduct ” by organized retail for dealing 
with small suppliers. These may then be incorporated into enforceable legislation. 
 7. Simplification of the licensing and permit  regime for organized retail and move towards 
a nationwide uniform licensing regime in the States to facilitate modern retail. 
 8. Strengthening the Competition Commission’s role for enforcing rules against collusion 
and predatory pricing. 
 9. Modernization of APMC markets as modelled on the National Dairy Development Board 
(NDDB) Safal market in Bangalore.

of US$ 200 Billion, fixed at the time of announcement of Foreign Trade Policy on 11th April, 2008,

Gems and Jewellery, Leather and Leather products, Marine, Textile, Handloom, Carpets,

†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 89 
 (c) how Government proposes to check that money which comes in the form of Foreign

route? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRIAL POLICY AND 
PROMOTION, MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR): (a) As 
per the extant policy, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) can be brought into the country through 
the following two methods:— 
 Procedure under Automatic Route: 
 FDI in sectors/activities to the extent perm itted under automatic route does not require any 
prior approval either by the Government or Re serve Bank of India (RBI). The investors are 
only required to notify the Regional office co ncerned of RBI within 30 days of receipt of 
inward remittances and file the required docume nts with that office within 30 days of issue 
of shares to foreign investors. 
 Procedure under Government Approval:  
 FDI in activities covered under the approval  route, requires prior Government approval. 
Such proposals are considered by the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB), 
through an inter-ministerial consultation process. 
 Applications for all FDI cases, except Non- Resident Indian (NRI) investments, Export 
Oriented Units (EOUs) and for FDI in retail trading of single branded products are required 
to be submitted to the FIPB Unit, Department  of Economic Affairs (DEA), Ministry of 
Finance. 
 Applications for NRI investment, EOU and for FD I in retail trading of single branded products 
should be submitted to the Secretariat for Indu strial Assistance (SIA) in the Department of 
Industrial Policy and Promotion. 
 Applications can also be submitted with Indi an Missions abroad wh o forward them to the 
DEA for further processing. 
 Cases for FDI coming through non-resident enti ties in Dubai, which fall under the approval 
route also require prior approval of FIPB, as in the case of similar investments from any 
other country. 
 (b) No Sir, excepting the procedure as mentioned at (a) above. 
 (c) The policy on FDI is incorporated in th e Foreign Exchange Management (Transfer or 
Issue of Security by a Person Resident Outside India) Regulations, 2000, notified under the 
Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999. FEMA indicates the countries from where 
investment is not permitted. As per Section 5(1) of these FEMA Regulations mentioned above, a 
person resident outside India, other than any entity in Pakistan, may purchase shares or 
convertible debentures of an Indian comp any under FDI Scheme, subject to terms and 
conditions specified in Schedu le I. FDI coming from Bangladesh is required to follow  
the approval route. Section 13 of the Act provides for imposition of penalty, after adjudication, for 

 90 
contravention of the provisions of the Act or Rules/Regulations. Further, any company 
established in the country has to follow the releva nt rules and regulations and is subject to the 
provisions of relevant Acts, including the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.

Bangladesh, geographical proximity, family ties  and ethnic similarity, coupled with better

comprehensive measures are essential to check this clandestine activity. 
 Hon’ble Supreme Court of India has issued  some direction in the Writ Petition

state-wise, is not available. However, a comprehe nsive set of measures have been put in place 
by the Government to deal with issue in the country, including Assam.

Steps to resolve border disputes between States 
 919. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
  DR. JANARDHAN WAGHMARE: 
 Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether the Union Government is aware that border disputes amongst some States 
are continuing since the past several decades; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; 
 (c) whether the border disputes amon gst some States have increased; and 
 (d) if so, the steps taken by the Union Government to resolve such border disputes? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (DR. SHAKEEL 
AHMAD): (a) and (b) Maharashtra — Karnataka — Kerala:  
 The boundary dispute between Karnataka and Maharashtra relate s to the claim of 
Karnataka for the transfer of contiguous Kannada-speaking areas in Maharashtra to 
Karnataka and the claim of Maharashtra for transfer of Marathi-speaking areas in Karnataka 
to Maharashtra. Karnataka has also claimed the Taluka of Kasargod in Kerala. The dispute 
is persisting since 1956. Kerala had not accepted the claim of Karnataka. The Governments 
of Maharashtra and Karnataka have taken opposite stands on the recommendations of the 
Mahajan Commission, which had been constituted by the Union Government with a view to 
settle the boundary dispute. 
Punjab — Haryana  
 The dispute between Punjab and Haryana from 1966 pertains to the transfer of Chandigarh 
to Punjab and part of Fazilka Tehsil of Punjab to Haryana. 

 110 
Assam — Nagaland  
 The Government of Assam has filed an Original Suit in the Supreme Court of India under 
Article 131 of the Constitution for demarcation of its boundaries on the ground. The 
Supreme Court in its Judgment dated 25.9.2006 has appointed a Local Commission for 
identification of the boundaries of Assam — Nagaland. The Local Commission is continuing 
with its hearings. 
Assam — Arunachal Pradesh  
 The Government of Assam has filed an Original Suit in the Supreme Court of India under 
Article 131 of the Constitution for demarcation of its boundaries on the ground. The 
Supreme Court in its Judgment dated 25.9.2006 has appointed a Local Commission for 
identification of the boundaries of Assam — Arunachal Pradesh. The Local Commission is 
continuing with its hearings. 
Assam — Meghalaya  
 There is some boundary dispute between A ssam and Meghalaya. Th e Central Government 
has advised both State Governments from time to time to resolve the matter through mutual 
understanding. 
Assam — Mizoram  
 The Government of Mizoram has requested the Central Government to constitute a 
separate Boundary Commission to resolv e the Assam-Mizoram boundary dispute.  
The Central Government has sought comments of State Government of Assam in this 
regard. 
Andhra Pradesh — Orissa, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry  
 As per available information, the State of Andhra Pradesh has boundary disputes with 
Orissa, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Na du and Puducherry. None of these State 
Governments have approached the Central Government to resolve their boundary disputes. 
Orissa — Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal  
 The State of Orissa, as per available inform ation, has boundary disputes with Jharkhand 
(earlier Bihar), Chhattisgarh (formerly Madhya Pradesh) and West Bengal. None of these 
State Governments have approached the Cent ral Government to resolve their boundary 
disputes. 
Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh 
 As per available information, there are boun dary disputes between Uttarakhand (formerly 
Uttar Pradesh) and Himachal Pradesh. However neither of the State Governments has 
approached the Central Government to resolve their boundary disputes. 
 (c) and (d) The approach of the Central Govern ment has consistently been that inter State 
boundary disputes can be resolved only with the willing cooperation of the State Governments 

 111
concerned and that the Central Government works only as a facilitator for amicable settlement of 
the dispute in a spirit of mutual accommodatio n and understanding. The Central Government 
had constituted the Mahajan Commission in October, 1966 to resolve the Maharashtra-
Karnataka-Kerala boundary dispute. Three Commissions have so far been appointed to 
determine the areas of Punjab that should go to  Haryana in lieu of Chandigarh. Government of 
India has made efforts in the past to reso lve the boundary dispute between Assam and 
Nagaland, but these efforts were in vain.

Checking human smuggling 
 932. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to  
state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that human smugglin g can be described as an organized crime in 
India and thus helping the touts to earn in lakhs; 
 (b) if so, the States involved and number of smuggling of humans took place during the last 
three years, State-wise; 

 123
 (c) whether Government has taken any steps so  far to combat the situation and also to 
check the easy availability of immigrant licences; and 
 (d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (DR. SHAKEEL 
AHMAD): (a) and (b) The Policy Planning Group (T wenty) formed by Ministry of Home Affairs 
in 1999 has identified 31 Criminal Activities to be defined as Organized Crime. The National Crime 
Records Bureau (NCRB) is impl ementing a project known as the Organized Crime Intelligence 
System (OCIS). ‘Human smuggling’ does not figu re in the category of organized crime in the 
NCRB database. Data and information on human sm uggling is not being maintained centrally as 
all illegal migration of people need not necessarily  imply trafficking in persons. Even Ministry of 
Overseas Indian Affairs has no data on huma n smuggling and the numb er of smuggling cases 
State-wise 
 (c) and (d) The Ministry of Overseas Indian  Affairs administers the Emigration Act, 1983. 
The steps taken to combat the situation are given in enclosed Statement. 
Statement 
Steps taken by Government to combat the situation and to check the 
easy availability of immigrant licences 
 Under the provisions of the said Act, the Pr otector General of Emigrants and the Protectors 
of Emigrants are concerned with those who go abroad for employment after obtaining emigration 
clearances from the Protectors of Emigrants. Further, under the provisions of the Act, 
registration certificates are issued to recruiting agents for conducting the business of recruitment 
overseas. Such agents recruit wo rkers for jobs abroad and are to follow the due procedure as 
prescribed in the Act and the rules made thereunder. 
 Complaints are received in the Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs and Indian Missions 
regarding duping of workers by unscrupulous agen cies by extorting large sums of money and 
sending them for employment on visit visas or even transit visas. Complaints are also  
received regarding non-payment of salary, longer work hours, lack of proper accommodation, 
food and medical facilities and ill-treatment in  other forms. In such  cases, if registered 
recruitment agency is involved, action is taken under the provisions of the Emigration Act, 
1983, leading to suspension and cancellation of th eir registration certific ates (RC). In respect 
of unregistered recruiting agents, the complaints are referred to concerned State Police 
Authorities/Protector of Emigrants for investigation and appropriate action as per provisions of 
the law. 
 The Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs takes action against the regist ered recruiting agents 
and unregistered agents for violation of the prov isions of the Emigration Act on the basis of 
complaints received. The State Governments (State Police Authorities) also take action directly 
in most of the cases which come to their notice.

Law and order situation in NCR 
 933. SHRI N.K. SINGH: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that law and orde r has been worsening in some parts of NCR 
making it difficult for women to perform even th e routine chores with police becoming a silent 
spectator; and 
 (b) the action Government has taken to rest ore confidence of the people in the law and 
order machinery and enable them to perform their day to day work? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V. RADHIKA 
SELVI): (a) and (b) As per the Constitution, “Public Order” is a State subject, and it is primarily 
the responsibility of the State Governments to maintain law and order in their States. The, 
Central Government, however, monitors law and order situation in the country on a regular 
basis, and in the process, maintains close co ntact with State Governments besides sharing 
information with them. Whenever necessary, advisories are also sent to the State Governments. 
When necessary, the Central Government, on th e request of the State Government (s) also 
provides assistance in the from of deployment of  Central para-military forces to aid States to 
effectively deal with any specific situation that may arise. 
Cyber crimes on rise 
 †934. SHRI BRIJ BHUSHAN TIWARI: Will the Mi nister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that cyber cr ime is growing very fast in the world; 
 (b) whether these crimes are on  the rise in India too; and 
 (c) if so, the action being taken by Government for its prevention? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (DR. SHAKEEL 
AHMAD): (a) The National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), which compiles State-wise data on 
various crimes in India under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and Indian Penal Code 
(IPC), does not have any comparable data to comment on the prevailing cyber crime scenario in 
the world. 
 (b) As per information compiled by NCRB, during the years 2005, 2006 and 2007, a total of 
179, 142 and 217 cases were registered in the co untry under the Information Technology Act, 
2000 and a total of 302, 311 and 339 cases were re gistered in the country under cyber crime 
related Sections of the IPC, respectively. 
 (c) The existing Information Technology Act, 2000 provides for legal framework to prevent 
cyber crimes. Further, the Act has been amended to include provisions to address computer 
crimes like phishing, spamming, online frauds and identity theft as also for data protection. The 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 125
Department of Information Technology (DIT) has set up Resource Centre for Cyber Forensics 
at the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC), Thiruvanathapuram, which 
has developed indigenous cyber forensic tools. These tools are now being used by agencies 
to investigate cyber crime cases. The C-DAC, Thiruvanathapuram also conducts training 
programmes for law enforcement agencies on these tools. The Indian Computer Emergency 
Response Team(CERT-In) provides reactive and proactive support to the cyber incidents in 
the country. It also liaisons with similar agencies worldwide and users of cyber space in  
the country including Government, public or private and issues alerts, advisories and 
vulnerability notes. These advisories are also published on the website of CERT-In 
(http://www.cert-in.org.in). The CERT-In also interacts with cyber users in the country to 
mitigate such incidents. 
 Organizations like Police Academies, Centra l Bureau of Investigation (CBI), Indian 
Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), Controller of Certifying Authority (CCA), 
NCRB, Regional Police Computer Training Centres (RPCTCs) etc. also conduct regular training 
programmes for imparting training to the police officials for preventing cyber crimes in the 
country. The Department of Information Techno logy (DIT) has provided grants to Central 
Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and Kerala Police to set up Cyber forensic labs for investigation of 
cyber crimes and these labs will also be used for training of police officers. Three Central 
Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs) and three Government Examiners of Questioned 
Documents Laboratories (GEsQD) under the Directorate of Forensic Science (DFS) are having 
good facilities for providing forens ic analytical support to the in vestigating agencies to handle 
cyber crimes through digital evidence. These laboratories under the DFS regularly conduct 
training programmes throughout the year for the benefit of law enforcement agencies and train 
them in search and seizure methods for handlin g cyber crimes and Internet crimes, e-mail 
investigations, mobile phone forensics etc.. The Government has also conducted several 
awareness and training programmes on cyber laws  and cyber crimes for Judicial officers and 
Law Enforcement Agencies. 
 Further, under the Plan Scheme of Eleventh Fi ve Year Plan of the Directorate of Forensic 
Science (DFS), for improving the facilities and training in handling cases of cyber crime, 
Information Technology etc. of Directorate of Forensic Science, there is a Scheme titled 
‘Creation of National Training and Resource Centre for Cyber Forensics’, with an outlay of Rs. 10 
crore.

Undue delay in FCRA approvals 
 943. DR. V. MAITREYAN: Will the Minister  of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that huge number of applications for approval of prior permission 
and permanent number under the Foreign Contri butions Regulation Act are pending in the 
Ministry for more than a year and above; 
 (b) the reasons for this undue delay in granting permissions under the Foreign 
Contributions Regulation Act; 
 (c) the steps being taken to improve the system; and 
 (d) the total number of such applications se parately under prior permission and permanent 
numbers pending for more than a year and above in the department? 

 134
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SRIPRAKASH 
JAISWAL): (a) to (d) On an average, about 4000 to 5000 applications seeking registration and 
prior permission under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976 are received from 
Associations in a year. Registration or prior permission is granted after due scrutiny of 
applications and a field verification of antecedents and activities of the applicant Association and 
its office bearers. A concerted attempt is ma de to process each and every case with due 
expedition. However, in certain cases, it may take  a longer time to process applications mainly 
due to deficient or incorrect information furnished by Association, detected during scrutiny of the 
application and/or the field ve rification report, which necessitates obtaining additional 
Information from the Association to facilitate a judicious evaluation of the application before a 
considered decision is taken. 
 Under the normal circumstances, registration under the Act is granted in four to eight 
months from the date of receipt of applicatio n while prior permission is granted within the 
prescribed time limit of three to four months. However, in those prior permission cases, where 
the amount of foreign contribution sought is ab ove a prescribed threshold limit, the antecedents 
of the foreign donor are also required to be verified, which is a time consuming activity. 
 As per information available, as against a to tal number of about 3800 applications received 
for registration/prior permission during the year 2007, about 450 applications are still in different 
stages of processing, mainly on account of information awaited from the applicant 
Association/field agency. 
 To put in place a user-friendly system, ‘FCR A On-Line’ services have been introduced, 
both for registration and prior permission, whic h has rationalized processing time to improve

 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SRIPRAKASH 
JAISWAL): (a) In the year 2000, the policy relating to grant of Indian citizenship to Afghan

 (i) Every person born in India between 26.01.1950 to 30.06.1987 is a citizen of India;

India provided either of his/her parents is a citizen of India;

 (c) Details of the observed and projected changes in the climate were first reported in

Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in June, 2004. This effort has been

agencies.

which has been the basis of all past analyses of climate change and variability. The IITM, Pune is

region using a regional model developed by the Hadley Centre of the UK Met. Office.

Job loss due to recession 
 960. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: 
  SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: 
 Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether 5 lakhs persons have lost their jobs in the last 3 months in our country; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof, sector-wise; and 
 (c) the action taken to ensure that no empl oyee would lose his job due to recession? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINI STRY OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT  
(SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. With a view to assess impact of economic 
slowdown on employment in the industries/sectors presumed to be adversely affected by the 
slowdown during the quarter October-December, 2008, Ministry of Labour and Employment 
carried out a survey in important sectors, viz. Mining, Textiles, Metals, Gems and Jewellery, 
Automobile, Transport and IT/BPO. These sectors contributed more than 60% to GDP in the 
year 2007-08. It has been revealed that about half a million workers have lost their jobs during 
October-December, 2008. Decrease in employment has been revealed in all the above sectors, 
except the IT/BPO sector, wherein it has shown a marginal increase (0.55 percent). Average 

 153
monthly decline in employment was highest (8. 58 percent) in Gems and Jewellery followed by 
Transport (4.03 percent), Automobiles (2.42 percent), Metals (1.91 percent), Textiles (0.91 
percent) and Mining (0.33 percent). The major impa ct of the slowdown is noticed in the export 
oriented units. 
 Department of Commerce, Government of In dia have been undertaking sample surveys 
relating to reduction in exports and resultant jo b losses in export-related industries. In the 
updated sample survey on jo b losses for export-related in dustries for August, 2008 to 16 
January, 2009, out of 402 units surveyed, the loss in export orders is around Rs. 6272 crores 
and loss of 1,09,513 jobs. 
 (c) Government is concerned about the impact  of global financial crisis on the Indian 
economy and several measures fina ncial and fiscal have been initiated to instil confidence in the 
economy, spur growth and overcome crisis. Some of the important steps relate to RBI measures 
to enhance liquidity in the market and two econ omic packages by the Government of India, 
mainly comprising additional spending, interest subvention and excise duty cuts. 
 In order to provide a social safety net, with effect from 01.04.2005, the Employees’ State 
Insurance Corporation has introduced “Rajiv Gandhi Shramik Kalyan Yojana ”. Under the 
scheme, employees who lose their employment due to retrenchment, closure of factories/ 
establishments or permanent invalidity due to non-employment injury, after being insured for five 
or more years, are entitled to Unemployment Allowance in cash equal to 50% of their wage upto 
1 year during his/her entire serv ice. In addition, he and his family members are also entitled to 
medical care.

 969. SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state:

year; 
 (b) if so, whether in addition over 50 million could lose jobs by end of 2009; 
 (c) whether many Indian employees in gulf ar e returning to India as a global recession and 
nearly 20,000 during last four months from UAE and also in just three months five lakhs workers 
were axed; 
 (d) if so, to what extent NREGA initiated by Government has been able to provide jobs to

 (e) what concrete steps and measures Government propose to take to meet situation? 

 162
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHANDRA 
SEKHAR SAHU): (a) and (b) No, Sir. There are no job cuts under NREGA. 
 (c) National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 is applicable in all the rural areas of 
the country. It is demand driven. The Act pr ovides for a legal guar antee of 100 days of 
employment to every rural household in a financial year whose adult members volunteer to do 
unskilled manual work. Thus, all rural households can apply for job under NREGA. 
 (d) NREGA was implemented in 200 identified di stricts in its first phase with effect from 
2.2.2006 and was extended to 130 additional districts in the second phase during 2007-08. All 
the remaining rural areas in the country have been covered under the Act with effect from 
1.4.2008. 2.10 crore households were provided employment under NREGA during 2006-07, 3.39 
crore households have been provided employment during 2007-08 and 3.81 crore have been 
benefited during 2008-09, up to January, 2009. 
 (e) Ministry has advised all States to clos ely monitor their programmes to ensure that 
atleast all BPL families willing to do unskilled manual work are covered under NREGA. Besides 
providing unskilled manual work, the Act also generates skilled jobs in the form of engineers, 
administrative officers, Assistants, Accountants, ICT personnel. States have been directed to 
deploy adequate number of dedicated staff with  the implementing agen cies. The Ministry has 
also insisted on 100% ICT facilities at Block level in terms of personnel, Computers, training by 
professional and connectivity.  The Ministry has allowed States to outsource work to 
professionals for technical support  on any of the programme aspects such as works, MIS, help 
lines, evaluation and studies. This can help generate employment for professionals in the 
market. 
 NREGA Guidelines permit one time expenses for non-recurring items like computers, 
printers, cupboards/office racks and other necess ary office equipments to facilitate proper 
maintenance of records and administrative functioning. All Blocks need to have computers 
dedicated to NREGA with required connectivity. All Gram Panchayats, Programme officers and 
District Programme Coordinator’s office are to have basic necessary office equipments. This will 
not only increase office efficiency but will al so give an impetus to local economy in the 
manufacturing sector.

Contaminated drinking water in rural areas 
 †977. SHRI PRABHAT JHA: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
 (a) whether Government has made any survey in regards of non-availability of drinking 
water and contaminated drinking water in villages; 
 (b) if so, the details of the survey; and 
 (c) the reasons for failure in providing clea n drinking water despite of commencing of 
scheme to provide pure drinking water in the villages? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHANDRA 
SEKHAR SAHU): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. A survey of all habitations and the status of drinking water 
supply was carried out by all States in 2003. As per the coverage status reported by the States in 
2003 and validated by Indian Institute of Public Administration, there were 2,47,943 Not Covered 
(NC), 3,89,409 Partially Covered (PC) and 8,69, 997 Fully Covered (FC) habitations. Each 
habitations is to be supplied the stipulated norm of 40 litres per capita per day (lpcd). However, 
coverage status is a dynamic one. Fully Covered habitations slip back to Partially Covered or Not 
Covered status due to various factors, viz., sources going dry due to lowering of ground water 
table, sources becoming quality affected, syst ems outliving their lives, systems working below 
rated capacity due to poor operation and maintenance, increase in population etc. Under Bharat 
Nirman, it is envisaged to cover all the uncovered as well as slipped back habitations in a period 
of four years starting from 2005-06 to 2008-09. 
Modernisation programme for national land records 
 978. SHRI MOHD. ALI KHAN: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
 (a) whether Government has initiated national land records modernisation programme in 
each State especially in Andhra Pradesh; and 
 (b) if so, the details thereof and the prog ress made especially in Andhra Pradesh? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHANDRA 
SEKHAR SAHU): (a) and (b) Yes Sir, the National Land Records Modernization Programme 
(NLRMP) has been formulated by merging two Centrally-sponsored schemes of 
Computerization of Land Records (CLR) and Strengthening of Revenue Administration and 
Updating of Land Records (SRA and ULR). The NLRMP was approved by the Union Cabinet in 
its meeting held on 21.08.2008. The ultimate goal of the NLRMP is to usher in the conclusive 
titling system with title guarantee, to replace the current presumptive title system in the country. 
 The activities to be supported under the Programme, inter alia , include survey/resurvey 
using modern technology including aerial photogrammetry, updatin g of land records  
including mutation records, completion of comp uterization of the records of rights (RoRs), 
computerization of registration, automatic generation of mutation notices, digitization of maps,  
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 173
integration of the entire system and training an d capacity building of the concerned officials and 
functionaries. Connectivity amongst the land reco rds and registration offices and land records 
management centers at tehsil/taluk/circle/block level would also be supported. 
 Under the Programme, the Central Government will provide financial assistance to the 
States — 100% for the components of computerization of textual and spatial land records, 
training and capacity building, 50% for survey/resurvey and modern record rooms and 25% for 
computerization of registration offices and their connectivity to revenue offices. 
 The NLRMP is to be implemented in a time-bound manner and all the districts in the 
country are to be covered by the end of the Tw elfth Plan. Further, all the activities under the 
NLRMP are to converge in the district and district will be the unit of implementation. 
 A National-level Project/P roposal Sanctioning and Monitoring Committee has been 
constituted under the programme to, inter-alia, sanction the projects and proposals, provide 
suitable instructions for implementation of the programme, periodically monitor and review the 
progress of the implementation etc. The State/ UT proposals received for release of funds are 
being placed before the Committee. So far five meetings of the Committee have been held and 
proposals received from 16 States/UTs including Andhra Pradesh have been considered by  
the Committee and Rs. 237.26 crore has been sanctioned for release towards Central share. It 
has been decided to release 75% of the total sanctioned amount of Central share as 1st 
instalment. Accordingly, funds to the tune of Rs. 177.57 crore have been released as 1st 
instalment to 16 States/UTs including Andhra Pradesh so far, as per details given in the enclosed 
Statement.

Sale of acquired land to private companies 
 †980. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister  of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
 (a) whether Government is aware that land of  farmers is acquired in various States and 
after the lapse of many years and achieving of the objectives of acquisition the land is not handed 
over to farmers after making it free from acquisition; 
 (b) whether at many places, such acquired land  is being sold to big private establishments 
and companies by Government at high prices by charging its land use; 
 (c) whether Government proposes to bring any bill to protect the farmers from such 
exploitation by State Governments; and 
 (d) if so, the outline of the bill and if not, the reasons therefor? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHANDRA 
SEKHAR SAHU): (a) and (b) Land and its management are under the exclusive legislative and 
administrative jurisdiction of the States as provided in Entry No. 18 of List II (State List) of the 
Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. Acquisition of Agricultural Land for various projects of 
Union and State Governments is being done by the concerned State Governments. However, 
the Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development has formulated a revised 
National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Polic y (NRRP), 2007, which was approved by the 
Cabinet on 11th October, 2007, and the same have been published in the Gazette of India dated 
31st October, 2007. 
 The para 6.24.2 of the NRRP, 2007 provides that  if land compulsorily acquired for a project 
or part thereof, remains unutilized for the project for a period of five years from the date of taking 
over the possession by the requiring body, the same shall revert to the possession and 
ownership of the appropriate Government without payment of any compensation or 
remuneration to the requiring body. 
 (c) and (d) It has also been decided to give a statutory backing to the National 
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007 (N RRP-2007). Accordingly, the Rehabilitation and 
Resettlement Bill, 2007 and The Land Acquisitio n (Amendment) Bill, 2007 have been developed 
on the lines of the provisions of the Nation al Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007 and 
have been introduced in the Parliament during Winter season of 2007. However, the Bills were 
referred to the Standing Committee on Rura l Development. The Standing Committee has 
submitted its reports. The official amendment to these Bills have been developed by this 
Department in consultation with the Ministry of Law. These Bills were considered by the Cabinet 
and have been referred to the Group of Ministers for consideration.

Disparity in minimum wages in different States under NREGA 
 986. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) whether different minimu m wages in different States encourage the migration; and 

 183
 (b) whether NREGA could bring a parity in minimum wages and include all NREGA worker 
in social security schemes like EPF, ESIC, gratuity and pension? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHANDRA 
SEKHAR SAHU): (a) Minimum wages prevalent in  a State are fixed by the respective State 
Governments under Minimum Wages Act, 1948. No  case of encouraged migration have been 
reported so far due to different minimum wages in different States. 
 (b) Initially, the wage rate for agricultural labourers notified by th e States under Minimum 
Wages Act was adopted as wage rate under NREG A in accordance with Section 6(2) of NREG 
Act. Central Government has notified wa ge rate under NREGA for different States  vide  
notification dated 1st January, 2009. 
 Aim of NREGA is to enhance livelihood security  in rural areas by providing at least 100 days 
of guaranteed wage employment in a financia l year to every household whose adult members 
volunteer to do unskilled manual work. Benefits like EPF, ESIC, Pension and gratuity are 
available to the workers of organized sector. NREGA workers are casual workers and do not 
belong to any organized sector. Therefore, the benefits of EPF, ESIC, Pension and Gratuity are 
not extendable to NREGA workers. However, in order to ensure that NREGA workers are also 
provided with social security sc hemes in addition to benefits already available under the Act, 
Government has decided to  include them under the “Rural Poor ” Category of Janshree Bima 
Yojana and to extend the benefits of Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana.

Clean drinking water to rural areas 
 988. SHRI B.S. GNANADESIKAN: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased 
to state: 
 (a) whether 80 per cent of people in our countr y especially in rural areas do not have an 
access to clean drinking water and 37.7 million people are affected by water borne diseases; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; 
 (c) whether it is a fact that 1.5 million children die due to diarrhoea every year and 21 per 
cent of communicable diseases in the country due to unsafe water; 
 (d) whether Government spends Rs. 6700 crores  on treatment on water borne diseases in 
rural areas; and 
 (e) if so, the details thereof and steps ta ken by Government to prevent water borne 
diseases and provide clean drinking water to rural areas? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHANDRA 
SEKHAR SAHU): (a) to (c) According to a report entitled ‘Safe Water, Better Health’ published 
in 2008 by the World Health Organization (WHO), 86% of the population in India has been 
provided with improved water facility. Accord ing to the same report, 88 per cent cases of 
diarrhoea world-wide are attributable to unsafe water, inadequate sanitation or insufficient 
hygiene. These cases result in about 1.5 million  deaths every year, most being the deaths of 
children. The category “diarrhea” includes some more severe diseases, such as cholera, typhoid 
and dysentery, all of which have related “faecal-oral” transmission pathways. Children 
particularly in developing countries suffer a di sproportionate share of disease burden due to 
water, sanitation and hygiene. The fraction of total deaths or DALYs (disability adjusted life year) 
attributable to unsafe water, inadequate sanitation or hygiene is more than 20% in children upto 
14 years of age. 
 (d) and (e) Government has taken a number of steps to enable the people to have access 
to safe drinking water and prevent water borne diseases. For improving health of people living in 

 185
rural areas, Government of India has launched Na tional Rural Health Mission (NRHM) for which 
budgetary provision of Rs. 12,050 crore has been made in 2008-09, inter-alia which includes 
provision for treatment of people suffering with water borne diseases. Similarly, to enable the 
people living in rural areas to have access to safe  drinking water, Government of India provides 
financial assistance to States under Accele rated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP), 
which is major component of Bharat Nirman. Tot al Sanitation Campaign (TSC) has also been 
launched to improve the sanitation in rural areas. During 2008-09, budgetary provision of Rs. 
7,400 core for rural water supply and Rs. 1.200 crore for sanitation have been made. 
 To generate awareness about various aspects rela ting to safe drinking water and enable the 
rural community to monitor the quality of drinking  water, National Rural Drinking Water Quality 
Monitoring and Surveillance programme has been  launched in the year 2006 and so far Rs. 
242.53 crore has been released to all the St ates/UTs for various programme activities inter-alia 
which includes awareness generation, procurement of water testing kits, training of 5 persons in 
each Gram Panchayat, 5 persons in each Block Panchayat, 4 persons in-each Zila Panchayat 
and 2 persons at the State level for carrying out water quality monitoring and surveillance 
activities. As reported by the States/UTs so fa r, 2,46,200 persons have been imparted training 
under the programme.
